text: In the proof, why does `trouble` produce a contradiction in both cases?
choices: Because `trouble` never terminates, which makes `halts(trouble, trouble)` undefined.
Because passing a program its own text is not legal, so the construction is ill-formed.
Because `halts` must simulate `trouble`, which simulates `halts`, and the recursion never ends.
It does the opposite of what `halts` predicts, so a correct prediction is self-defeating either way.
explanation: If `halts` says it halts, `trouble` loops; if `halts` says it loops, `trouble` halts. `trouble` is built from `halts` by ordinary programming — a call, an `if`, a loop — so the only assumption that can be wrong is that `halts` exists. Passing a program its own text is perfectly legal: a program is a string, which is Unit VI's thesis and the reason this proof comes after Chapter 25.
